newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS-Resurgent ISS sees U.S. comeback.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Resurgent ISS sees U.S. comeback.

text.p: Danish cleaning group International Service System (ISS) on Tuesday put the disasters of 1996 firmly behind it, with solid first-half 1997 results and a bullish outlook on the future.

Posting profit of 83 million crowns ($11.9 million) compared to a loss of 2.02 billion in the first six months of 1996, the group predicted steady growth. ISS also said it was shopping for acquisitions and predicted that it could regain a U.S. presence in five years.
The 1996 losses were caused by falsified accounting at U.S. unit ISS Inc, which it sold last March to Canada's Aaxis Ltd for one dollar and a 19.5 percent stake in Aaxis.

"If things work out as we hope, and we believe they will, it would be very natural to try to acquire the majority of the company in, whatever it takes, five years time," ISS Managing Director Waldemar Schmidt told Reuters Financial Television.

In Tuesday's results ISS reported first-half turnover of 5.75 billion crowns, up from 5.32 billion during the first six months of 1996, and an increase in operating profit before other income and expenses of 268 million crowns, up from 241 million.
It forecast an eight percent full year rise for both.

"We are in a very strong position, not only in terms of having shown 10 percent growth...in the first six months of the year, we've also improved our operating result by 12 percent, so it's like margin improvement," Schmidt said in the interview.
"More fundamentally we have improved our financial position. Our equity ratio has increased and we expect by the end of the year to have a more than 25 percent equity ratio," he added.

In later comments to Reuters he said that of the 10 percent growth, about six percent was organic and the rest generated by acquisitions and foreign exchange gains. Of full-year 1997's eight percent overall growth, five percent would be organic.
Schmidt said that ISS, now equipped with a 700 million crown funding facility from Unibank was on the lookout for firms to buy, particularly in Germany, France and Asia.
"We could today write a cheque for a hundred million U.S. dollars for acquisitions and we are constantly looking, and currently looking, at acquisition possibilities," he said.
"We will concentrate our effort on medium sized and small acquisitions, as we did, for instance, in 1995 when we acquired about 30 companies."
In the wake of the ISS Inc sale, Schmidt said that the group might take its thinly-traded share off the New York market.
"We only have 0.3 percent of our share capital in the ADR programme and the trading volume is extremely low, we're talking about a few hundred shareholders," he added.
He said that the majority of U.S. and Canadian investors bought the Copenhagen-listed b-share.
"So the likelihood is that we at the end of the year will come to the conclusion that we might de-list (in New York)."
ISS said earlier that it was considering selling its British supply house ISS Darenas Ltd (U.K.) by the end of the year.
Last month it sold ISS Darenas International, which supplies cleaning materials and equipment to ISS companies and other clients in Scandinavia, to the Unilever group.

"ISS has been approached by several parties interested in acquiring ISS Darenas Ltd (U.K.)," ISS said. "If satisfactory terms can be obtained it is possible that ISS Darenas Ltd (U.K.) will be divested by the end of the year, thus increasing ISS Europe's ability to grow by selected acquisitions."

It did not name prospective buyers but said that income from the sale of ISS Darenas International would contribute a "substantial gain" to its second-half 1997 results. --Copenhagen newsroom +339695650 ($ = 6.986 Danish Crowns)
